intro.title: kube-sched-advisor
lines: Describe a workload in plain English. Get a scheduling plan from your live cluster.
Recorded on a real Amazon EKS cluster. No narration: each step has a caption.
Two real NVIDIA A10G nodes. The H100 nodes are stand-ins: CPU nodes that advertise 8 GPUs.

steps.caption: The ask, in plain English: a 2-node, 8-GPU fine-tune that must start all at once.
steps.command: python -m sched_advisor suggest --brief --name gang-finetune "2 nodes x 8 H100 GPUs per node, NVLink, all-or-nothing fine-tune, 1 cpu and 1 GiB per pod"
steps.output:
Recommended: Secondary scheduler gang-scheduler (scheduler-plugins Coscheduling + GPU bin-packing)

Why:
  - Pin to nvidia.com/gpu.product=NVIDIA-H100-80GB-HBM3 so the pod only lands on H100 nodes.
  - Add tolerations for GPU-node taints (taints keep CPU pods off GPUs; a toleration only allows
    placement, it does not attract the pod - the nodeSelector/requests do that).
  - No batch system is installed, so the lightest gang option is the Coscheduling plugin from
    kubernetes-sigs/scheduler-plugins.
  - It runs as a second scheduler: the default scheduler is untouched (required on EKS, where the
    default scheduler's config cannot be edited).

Findings:
  BLOCKER: No node can run even one pod.
  WARNING: Enough GPUs in total, but they are fragmented.
  WARNING: The gang cannot start right now under any scoring strategy.
  WARNING: No single network domain can host the whole job.
  NOTE: EKS: default scheduler config is not editable.

Simulation: default scheduler places 0/2 pods; no single network.topology/block has room for the
            whole job; 18 GPUs free, 0 whole nodes free

Manifests and the full report: out/gang-finetune/

section.title: Scenario 1: an all-or-nothing training job
section.subtitle: 2 nodes x 8 H100, on a pool that other teams have fragmented.

steps.caption: Check against the real kube-scheduler: one pod that wants a whole node. Same verdict as the advisor.
steps.command: kubectl apply -f demo/probe-pod.yaml && sleep 8 && kubectl get pod train-probe && kubectl get events --field-selector involvedObject.name=train-probe,reason=FailedScheduling -o custom-columns=MESSAGE:.message --no-headers

steps.caption: Same ask, new cluster state: both workers place, and the whole job fits inside one network block.
steps.command: python -m sched_advisor suggest --brief --name gang-finetune "2 nodes x 8 H100 GPUs per node, NVLink, all-or-nothing fine-tune, 1 cpu and 1 GiB per pod"
steps.output:
Recommended: Secondary scheduler gang-scheduler (scheduler-plugins Coscheduling + GPU bin-packing)

Why:
  - Pin to nvidia.com/gpu.product=NVIDIA-H100-80GB-HBM3 so the pod only lands on H100 nodes.
  - Add tolerations for GPU-node taints (taints keep CPU pods off GPUs; a toleration only allows
    placement, it does not attract the pod - the nodeSelector/requests do that).
  - No batch system is installed, so the lightest gang option is the Coscheduling plugin from
    kubernetes-sigs/scheduler-plugins.
  - It runs as a second scheduler: the default scheduler is untouched (required on EKS, where the
    default scheduler's config cannot be edited).

Findings:
  NOTE: EKS: default scheduler config is not editable.

Simulation: default scheduler places 2/2 pods; whole job fits in one network.topology/block:
            block-a; 22 GPUs free, 2 whole nodes free

Manifests and the full report: out/gang-finetune/

steps.caption: It wrote manifests. Ask the real API server to validate them. Nothing is created (server dry run).
steps.command: ls out/gang-finetune && kubectl create namespace research && kubectl apply --dry-run=server -f out/gang-finetune/00-priorityclass.yaml -f out/gang-finetune/30-workload.yaml

steps.caption: The plan also writes a PodGroup so both pods start together, and points the Job at the second scheduler.
steps.output:
apiVersion: scheduling.x-k8s.io/v1alpha1
kind: PodGroup
metadata:
  name: gang-finetune
  namespace: research
spec:
  minMember: 2
  scheduleTimeoutSeconds: 600
70:      schedulerName: gang-scheduler

steps.caption: A serving ask on the real GPUs. The advisor sees the GPU nodes are tainted and plans for it.
steps.command: python -m sched_advisor suggest --brief --name gpu-serve --image nvidia/cuda:12.4.1-base-ubuntu22.04 --command "sleep infinity" "serve a chat model, 2 replicas, 1 A10G GPU each, highly available, 1 cpu and 1 GiB per pod"
steps.output:
Recommended: Default kube-scheduler + spreading (Deployment, topology spread, PDB)

Why:
  - Pin to nvidia.com/gpu.product=NVIDIA-A10G so the pod only lands on A10G nodes.
  - Add tolerations for GPU-node taints (taints keep CPU pods off GPUs; a toleration only allows
    placement, it does not attract the pod - the nodeSelector/requests do that).
  - Serving needs availability, not packing: keep the default LeastAllocated scoring so replicas
    spread out and a single node failure costs one replica.
  - Topology spread across topology.kubernetes.io/zone is hard (DoNotSchedule) because this is
    critical.
  - A PodDisruptionBudget keeps node drains/Karpenter consolidation from taking out several replicas
    at once.

Simulation: default scheduler places 2/2 pods; 2 GPUs free, 2 whole nodes free

Manifests and the full report: out/gpu-serve/

section.subtitle: The two real A10G nodes. The plan is applied for real.

steps.caption: Both real GPUs are now taken. A batch ask for 4 more GPU workers, and the advisor says so.
steps.command: python -m sched_advisor suggest --brief --name evals "batch eval job with 4 workers, 1 A10G GPU each, 1 cpu and 1 GiB per pod"
steps.output:
Recommended: Indexed Job

Why:
  - Pin to nvidia.com/gpu.product=NVIDIA-A10G so the pod only lands on A10G nodes.
  - Add tolerations for GPU-node taints (taints keep CPU pods off GPUs; a toleration only allows
    placement, it does not attract the pod - the nodeSelector/requests do that).
  - Pods are independent (no all-reduce), so gang semantics are unnecessary; each index can retry on
    its own (backoffLimitPerIndex).

Findings:
  BLOCKER: No node can run even one pod.

Simulation: default scheduler places 0/4 pods; 0 GPUs free, 0 whole nodes free

Manifests and the full report: out/evals/

section.title: Scenario 4: the platform team installs Kueue
section.subtitle: The advisor notices and changes its plan.

steps.caption: A shared-pool ask on the same cluster. The plan now uses Kueue queues instead of a second scheduler.
steps.command: python -m sched_advisor suggest --brief --name gang-kueue "2 nodes x 8 H100 GPUs per node, NVLink, all-or-nothing fine-tune, shared pool with other teams, 1 cpu and 1 GiB per pod"
steps.output:
Recommended: Kueue admission (all-or-nothing quota) + Topology-Aware Scheduling + gpu-binpack bin-
             packing profile

Why:
  - Pin to nvidia.com/gpu.product=NVIDIA-H100-80GB-HBM3 so the pod only lands on H100 nodes.
  - Add tolerations for GPU-node taints (taints keep CPU pods off GPUs; a toleration only allows
    placement, it does not attract the pod - the nodeSelector/requests do that).
  - Kueue keeps the Job suspended until quota for all workers is available, then admits it as a
    unit.
  - A ClusterQueue per team inside a shared cohort gives fair sharing: idle quota is borrowable and
    reclaimed with preemption when its owner needs it back.
  - Topology-Aware Scheduling: the pod-set annotation asks Kueue to place every worker inside one
    network.topology/block (required - simulation found block-a fits).
  - gpu-binpack uses MostAllocated with nvidia.com/gpu weight 5: fill GPU nodes before touching
    empty ones, so whole nodes stay free for big jobs and idle nodes can be scaled down.

Findings:
  NOTE: EKS: default scheduler config is not editable.

Simulation: default scheduler places 2/2 pods; whole job fits in one network.topology/block:
            block-a; 22 GPUs free, 2 whole nodes free

Manifests and the full report: out/gang-kueue/
